ocar.opportunity: The adult Drosophila melanogaster central brain connectome, with more than 125,000 neurons and 50 million synaptic connections, gives a whole-brain template for asking how sensory information is transformed into motor output.
ocar.challenge: A wiring diagram alone does not specify dynamics: each fly neuron can contact hundreds of partners, and it is unclear whether synapse counts plus predicted transmitter identity are enough to recover complete sensorimotor transformations.
ocar.action: Shiu, Sterne, Spiller, Franconville, Sandoval, Zhou, Simha, Kang, Yu, Kim, Dorkenwald, Matsliah, Schlegel, Yu, McKellar, Sterling, Costa, Eichler, Bates, Eckstein, Funke, Jefferis, Murthy, Bidaye, Hampel, Seeds, and Scott build a leaky integrate-and-fire model of the entire FlyWire brain in Brian2, using connectivity and neurotransmitter identity, with baseline firing of 0 Hz, to study feeding and grooming circuits.
ocar.resolution: Activating sugar- or water-sensing gustatory neurons predicted taste-responsive cells required for feeding initiation; activating feeding-region neurons predicted motor-neuron drivers that they validated with optogenetics and behavior. The same model recovered antennal grooming responses to mechanosensory subtypes. Across 164 empirically tested predictions, 91% were consistent (84% after excluding split-GAL4 experiments in which most cell types did not drive MN9).
ocar.future_work: They suggest more complete neurotransmitter and receptor annotations and more sophisticated morphology would improve later models.

summaries.beginner: A complete map of the fruit-fly brain still leaves open how those wires produce behavior. The authors built a computer model of every neuron firing and showed it can predict which cells drive feeding and grooming, then checked many of those predictions in real flies.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Shiu and colleagues construct a leaky integrate-and-fire model of the adult Drosophila central brain from the FlyWire connectome (>125,000 neurons, 50 million synapses) and predicted transmitters, simulated in Brian2 with 0 Hz baseline rates. Gustatory and mechanosensory activations recovered known feeding-initiation and antennal-grooming neurons and generated testable motor-neuron hypotheses that optogenetics confirmed. Of 164 empirically tested predictions, 91% matched experiment (84% excluding a split-GAL4 motor-neuron screen).
summaries.advanced: The model uses only synapse-level connectivity and predicted neurotransmitter identity; biophysical parameters are taken from prior literature and baseline rates are uniformly 0 Hz. Accuracy figures (91%/84%) mix circuit classes and depend on which predictions were testable. Morphology, receptors, and neuromodulation are flagged as missing. Catalog dimension is neuroai/modeling on fly, not a new EM volume.

plain_language_summary: A complete map of the fruit-fly brain still leaves open how those wires produce behavior. The authors built a computer model of every neuron firing and showed it can predict which cells drive feeding and grooming, then checked many of those predictions in real flies.

ocar.opportunity: Single-cell transcriptomics profiles gene expression by neuronal type, while connectomes quantify which types actually synapse, creating a chance to read a genetic code for wiring.
ocar.challenge: Which genes in pre- and postsynaptic partners jointly specify type-to-type connections remains hard to extract, especially in complex brains where many candidate adhesion and synapse genes co-vary.
ocar.action: Qiao proposes a bilinear model, analogous to a recommendation system, that maps presynaptic and postsynaptic expression into a covariance matrix trained to match an anatomical type-connectivity matrix.
ocar.resolution: On C. elegans electrical synapses the model performed comparably to, if slightly better than, the spatial connectome model (SCM), recovered all SCM genetic interactions and inferred additional ones. On mouse retina it recapitulated known bipolar-cell to retinal ganglion cell motifs and associated distinct motifs with adhesion and synapse-formation genes.
ocar.future_work: The preprint frames the method as a benchmark for transcriptomic analysis of synapses and as a starting point for mechanistic circuit-assembly and genetic-manipulation studies. Code is released at github.com/muqiao0626/Bilinear_Model.

summaries.beginner: Different kinds of brain cells wire to specific partners, but it is unclear which genes write those pairing rules. This paper trains a model that reads gene lists from both sides of a connection and tries to reconstruct who talks to whom.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2024 version of a 2023 preprint), Mu Qiao introduces bilinear modeling of neuronal-type connectivity from paired single-cell transcriptomes. Tested on C. elegans, it matched or slightly exceeded the spatial connectome model for reconstructing electrical synapses from expression and recovered all SCM-inferred genetic interactions plus extras. Applied to mouse retinal bipolar and ganglion cells, it reproduced recognized connectivity motifs and highlighted cell-adhesion and synapse-formation genes. Modeling code is public.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods preprint, not a causal gene knockout study. “Slightly better than SCM” is qualitative; no AUC or exact score appears in the selected text. Electrical-synapse reconstruction in worm is a different biological problem than chemical BC–RGC motifs in retina. Predicted partners in a supplementary table are only partly consistent with functional types. Catalog organisms are elegans and mouse.

plain_language_summary: Different kinds of brain cells wire to specific partners, but it is unclear which genes write those pairing rules. This paper trains a model that reads gene lists from both sides of a connection and tries to reconstruct who talks to whom.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric microscopy for connectomics, expansion microscopy, and live-cell imaging needs dense 3D instance labels, but those labels are the bottleneck that keeps specialist and generalist networks from being trained.
ocar.challenge: Dense expert annotation is prohibitive: the authors cite about 2,000 hours to densely label hippocampal neuropil in a 180 μm³ EM volume. 2D foundation models (SAM, microSAM, CellSAM, Cellpose, DINOv3) often fail on rare or complex EM structures, so 3D ground truth remains scarce.
ocar.action: Thiyagarajan, Sheridan, Harris, and Manor present a 2D→3D bootstrap: a 2D net trained on sparse labels completes boundaries on every section, and a 3D net pretrained on synthetic data infers inter-section connectivity. They validate across electron, expansion, and live-cell datasets and release Bootstrapper plus a Napari plugin.
ocar.resolution: 3D models trained on the resulting pseudo ground-truth reached accuracy comparable to dense expert labels, with up to a 1,000-fold cut in human annotation time; even with proofreading, total reconstruction cost dropped by an order of magnitude.
ocar.future_work: They argue the command-line tool is scriptable for AI agents that could run annotation–train–infer loops in parallel, and they flag a possible 3D-network modification to resolve remaining inter-section ambiguities.

summaries.beginner: Teaching a computer to color in every cell in a 3D microscope stack usually takes huge amounts of hand drawing. The authors show that a few 2D sketches plus a second network that links slices can stand in for that labor.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (catalog year 2024), Thiyagarajan, Sheridan, Harris, and Manor bootstrap dense 3D instance segmentations from sparse 2D labels. Motivation includes a 180 μm³ hippocampal EM volume that took about 2,000 expert hours to annotate densely. Across electron, expansion, and live-cell data, 3D models trained on pseudo ground-truth matched dense-expert accuracy with up to 1,000-fold less annotation time and about ten-fold lower total cost after proofreading. Code is at github.com/ucsdmanorlab/bootstrapper with a Napari plugin.
summaries.advanced: “Up to 1,000-fold” and “order of magnitude” are headline claims; dataset-wise scores are not in the selected extract. Pseudo ground-truth still needs proofreading. The PDF title differs slightly from the catalog row. Catalog stages include segmentation, proofreading, and infrastructure; organism is unspecified.

plain_language_summary: Teaching a computer to color in every cell in a 3D microscope stack usually takes huge amounts of hand drawing. The authors show that a few 2D sketches plus a second network that links slices can stand in for that labor.

ocar.opportunity: Brain-wide functional imaging in Drosophila can be compared across animals and labs, and aligned to gene-expression maps or connectomes, only if volumes share a common anatomical coordinate frame.
ocar.challenge: Registering in vivo multiphoton data to ex vivo atlases is hard because modality, microscope, and sample preparation all differ; many fly atlases therefore stay inside a single project’s apparatus.
ocar.action: Brezovec, Berger, Hao, Lin, Ahmed, Pacheco, Thiberge, Murthy, and Clandinin build an in vivo Functional Drosophila Atlas (FDA) from multiphoton brains and a two-step pipeline, BIFROST (BrIdge For Registering Over Statistical Templates), using ANTs linear and SyN plus dataset templates, to place functional data in FDA space and import ex vivo connectomes.
ocar.resolution: Using genetically labeled cell types as landmarks, they report registration precision of less than 10 microns across specimens and laboratories, and they demonstrate in-vivo to ultrastructural-connectome alignment.
ocar.future_work: The work positions BIFROST as enabling quantitative structure–function comparisons in future fly imaging studies.

summaries.beginner: Pictures of fly brains taken in different labs do not sit in the same coordinate system, so activity maps are hard to overlay on wiring diagrams. This paper builds a shared living-brain atlas and a registration pipeline that lines those pictures up to within a small fraction of a millimeter.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023; 2024 version in the extract), Brezovec, Berger, Hao, Lin, Ahmed and colleagues introduce the Functional Drosophila Atlas and BIFROST. The two-step pipeline uses ANTs linear and SyN registration and dataset templates to map in vivo volumes into FDA space and to bring in ex vivo resources such as connectomes. Genetically labeled landmarks (including LC11 glomeruli and DSX processes) yield sub-10-micron precision across animals and labs.
summaries.advanced: “Less than 10 microns” is a precision claim on genetically labeled landmarks, not a voxel-wise warping error for every neuropil. Supplementary analyses show centroid estimates depend on thresholding. This is a methods preprint. Catalog stages are preparation and alignment on fly.

plain_language_summary: Pictures of fly brains taken in different labs do not sit in the same coordinate system, so activity maps are hard to overlay on wiring diagrams. This paper builds a shared living-brain atlas and a registration pipeline that lines those pictures up to within a small fraction of a millimeter.

ocar.opportunity: Neuromodulators such as neuropeptides retune sensory networks to internal state, and the numerically small Drosophila antennal lobe (AL) is a tractable place to ask whether a widely distributed peptide acts uniformly.
ocar.challenge: Myoinhibitory peptide (MIP) looks uniform across AL glomeruli yet is implicated in satiation and post-mating odor preference, so a single peptide might still have stimulus- and glomerulus-specific effects.
ocar.action: Sizemore, Jonaitis, and Dacks combine anatomy, high-resolution connectomics, in vivo physiology, and receptor knockdown to test whether MIP uniformly modulates olfactory input.
ocar.resolution: A heterogeneous set of local interneurons is the sole AL MIP source. MIP decreases odor-evoked input in some glomeruli (e.g. DM2, DM5) and increases it in others (e.g. DM1, DM4). Differential expression of the inhibitory MIP receptor SPR, not LN wiring or odor responses, explains the split: SPR knockdown in olfactory sensory neurons abolishes the decreases but not the increases, which they attribute to disinhibition.
ocar.future_work: They sketch experiments to separate MIP from GABA in the same LNs, including chemogenetic LN activation with GAD1 knockdown.

summaries.beginner: A chemical messenger is spread evenly through the fly’s smell center, yet it turns some smell channels down and others up. The authors show that the difference comes from which cells carry the receptor, not from where the messenger is released.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2023), Sizemore, Jonaitis, and Dacks show that MIP, though uniform across the Drosophila antennal lobe, bidirectionally modulates glomerular olfactory input. Connectomics and physiology indicate heterogeneous MIPergic local neurons as the sole source; non-uniform SPR expression lets MIP act on distinct intraglomerular substrates. SPR knockdown in OSNs removes MIP-induced decreases in DM2 and DM5 (n=6) but not increases in DM1 and DM4 (n=7), supporting indirect disinhibition for the latter.
summaries.advanced: n values are small (Wilcoxon and repeated-measures ANOVA with Holm adjustment). “Sole source” is within the AL, not brain-wide. Increases after OSN SPR knockdown are interpreted as disinhibition, not proven by a full GABA-vs-MIP dissection. Catalog journal field says bioRxiv; the PDF is the published Nature Communications article. No pipeline stage is tagged.

plain_language_summary: A chemical messenger is spread evenly through the fly’s smell center, yet it turns some smell channels down and others up. The authors show that the difference comes from which cells carry the receptor, not from where the messenger is released.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can place Alzheimer’s-related molecules inside the complete local neuronal and glial milieu, linking amyloid-β (Aβ) and phosphorylated tau (pTau) to circuit structure.
ocar.challenge: Localizing specific biomolecules inside large vEM volumes has been difficult, especially without detergents that wreck ultrastructure, so connectomic context for plaques and tau has been limited.
ocar.action: Han, Li, Wang, Sanchez, Aggarwal, Blakely, Schalek, Meirovitch, Lin, Berger, Wu, Aly, Bay, Delatour, Lafaye, Pfister, Wei, Jain, Ploegh, and Lichtman use fluorescent nanobodies against pTau, Aβ, and the microglial marker CD11b in 3xTg mouse hippocampus, then register confocal maps to serial-section vEM (vCLEM) and release the volume publicly.
ocar.resolution: They report pTau-positive spine-like AIS protrusions innervated by axon terminals, AIS swellings and enlarged blebs, three reconstructed pyramidal neurons with intracellular Aβ or pTau, and automatic synapse detection showing synapse density and total synapse volume falling closer to an Aβ plaque.
ocar.future_work: They invite others to mine the public dataset and suggest the same nanobody vCLEM route for other molecules in animal or human dementia samples.

summaries.beginner: Alzheimer’s proteins are usually seen in glowing light-microscope stains, while wiring is seen in electron-microscope pictures, and the two rarely overlap. This study stains those proteins in a mouse hippocampus and then images the same piece of tissue in 3D electron microscopy so both can be studied together.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Han and colleagues present detergent-free nanobody vCLEM of Aβ, pTau, and CD11b in 3xTg hippocampus aligned to a large serial-section EM volume with segmented neurons, glia, and synapses. Proof-of-principle findings include pTau-positive spine-like protrusions at the axon initial segment and a decrease in synapse density and total synapse volume nearer an Aβ plaque. The dataset is released for community exploration.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods-and-resource preprint from one model (3xTg) and one hippocampal sample, not a population study of Alzheimer’s. AIS abnormalities are described from a few reconstructed cells; human-cortex comparison is qualitative. Automatic synapse detections near one plaque should not be generalized. Catalog tags mouse, segmentation, and electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: Alzheimer’s proteins are usually seen in glowing light-microscope stains, while wiring is seen in electron-microscope pictures, and the two rarely overlap. This study stains those proteins in a mouse hippocampus and then images the same piece of tissue in 3D electron microscopy so both can be studied together.

ocar.opportunity: Many motor systems drive distinct movements through one muscle set; Drosophila courtship song is a compact case, with males producing pulse and sine songs by vibrating the same wings.
ocar.challenge: How premotor circuits in the ventral nerve cord flexibly generate those two song modes—and how evolution layered a simpler song onto a more complex one—is not mapped at cellular and synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: Lillvis, Wang, Shiozaki, Xu, Stern, and Dickson combine cell-type-specific genetics, optogenetic activation and inhibition, calcium imaging, and the male ventral nerve cord (MANC) connectome to map song circuits and test each cell type’s contribution.
ocar.resolution: They report two nested feed-forward pathways with extensive reciprocal and feedback connections: a larger network produces pulse song (~220 Hz pulses every 35 ms), the more complex ancestral form, and a subset produces sine song (a continuous ~150 Hz hum), the simpler derived form.
ocar.future_work: They call for computational models that join this anatomy with physiology, and for voltage, transmitter, and holographic optogenetic measurements across the population.

summaries.beginner: Male fruit flies sing two different songs with the same wings. This paper maps the nerve-cord cells that make those songs and finds that the simpler song is made by a subset of the circuit that makes the more complex one.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Lillvis, Wang, Shiozaki, Xu, Stern, and Dickson reconstruct Drosophila melanogaster courtship-song circuits in the male VNC using split-GAL4 reagents and the MANC connectome. Pulse song is ~220 Hz pulses recurring every 35 ms; sine song is a ~150 Hz hum. The circuit is organized as nested feed-forward pathways with rich recurrence: the larger graph yields pulse song, a subset yields sine song. Activation and inhibition of each cell type were scored against song output.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint; MANC access is acknowledged as pre-release. Nested organization is an interpretation of anatomy plus perturbation, not a unique dynamical proof. Song-mode frequencies (~220 Hz, ~150 Hz, 35 ms) are literature values restated in the introduction. Catalog tags fly connectomics without a pipeline stage.

plain_language_summary: Male fruit flies sing two different songs with the same wings. This paper maps the nerve-cord cells that make those songs and finds that the simpler song is made by a subset of the circuit that makes the more complex one.

ocar.opportunity: Graph matching can pair bilaterally homologous neurons across hemispheres from connectivity alone, a practical need as connectomes grow.
ocar.challenge: Standard matching treats left and right as two isolated ipsilateral graphs and therefore throws away contralateral edges, which in a larval Drosophila subset are about 35% of edges picked at random.
ocar.action: Pedigo, Winding, Priebe, and Vogelstein modify a state-of-the-art matcher to solve bisected graph matching, using ipsilateral and contralateral subgraphs together, and combine it with earlier extensions that use edge types and known seeds.
ocar.resolution: Simulations and real connectomes show higher pairing accuracy when contralateral subgraphs are sufficiently edge-correlated; code and data are at github.com/neurodata/bgm and Zenodo.
ocar.future_work: They expect the bisected formulation to help future hemisphere pairing and other domains with the same block structure.

summaries.beginner: The two sides of a brain often contain matching cell types, and computers can guess those pairs from who connects to whom. This paper shows that connections that cross the midline, usually ignored, can make those guesses better.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2022), Pedigo, Winding, Priebe, and Vogelstein define bisected graph matching so contralateral as well as ipsilateral edges inform neuron pairing. They note that in a larval Drosophila connectome subset, a random edge is contralateral about 35% of the time. Accuracy improves when contralateral edge correlation is sufficient, and further gains come from typed edges and known pairs. Implementation is in graspologic-centered Python.
summaries.advanced: No numeric accuracy deltas appear in the selected extract beyond the 35% contralateral-edge observation. Gains are conditional on contralateral correlation. Padding is used when hemisphere sizes differ; an “adopted” padding scheme for weighted graphs was not explored. Organism is unspecified in the catalog despite fly examples.

plain_language_summary: The two sides of a brain often contain matching cell types, and computers can guess those pairs from who connects to whom. This paper shows that connections that cross the midline, usually ignored, can make those guesses better.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes predict function from anatomy, so a systematic functional map of signal flow is needed to test those predictions in a complete nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Anatomy does not specify sign, strength, timing, or extrasynaptic routes, and those properties may diverge from wired synapses.
ocar.action: Randi, Sharma, Dvali, and Leifer measure signal propagation in 23,427 neuron pairs across the C. elegans head by pairing optogenetic activation with whole-brain calcium imaging, including mutant tests of extrasynaptic signaling.
ocar.resolution: The functional atlas often differs from anatomical predictions. Dense-core-vesicle-dependent signals on seconds-or-less timescales evoke calcium transients, often without a direct wired edge but where relevant peptides and receptors are expressed. The measured atlas predicts spontaneous dynamics better than anatomy.
ocar.future_work: They conclude that synaptic and extrasynaptic signaling both drive short-timescale dynamics and that evoked-propagation maps are required to interpret function.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram of the worm brain does not by itself say how signals actually travel. The authors turned cells on one at a time and watched the rest of the head, building a map of who can make whom respond.
summaries.intermediate: In 2022 work catalogued without a journal field, Randi, Sharma, Dvali, and Leifer report a C. elegans head signal-propagation atlas from 23,427 optogenetically probed pairs with simultaneous whole-brain calcium imaging. Sign, strength, timing, and causal direction often depart from anatomy; mutants implicate extrasynaptic, dense-core-vesicle-dependent transmission on seconds-or-less timescales. The functional atlas outperforms anatomy at predicting spontaneous activity.
summaries.advanced: Selected PDF text did not match this paper (extract is an unrelated Twitter/politics review), so this annotation uses the catalog abstract only. Pair count 23,427 is from that abstract; no per-edge statistics or mutant genotypes are in the usable source. Venue is unspecified in the catalog row.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram of the worm brain does not by itself say how signals actually travel. The authors turned cells on one at a time and watched the rest of the head, building a map of who can make whom respond.

ocar.opportunity: None of the current EM neuron-segmentation methods is error-free, so connectomics still depends on proofreading merge and split mistakes.
ocar.challenge: Proofreading is usually interactive and manual, and merge and split errors often coexist in one volume, which sequential human workflows handle poorly.
ocar.action: Nguyen, Jang, Tuan, and Jeong introduce RLCorrector: hierarchical reinforcement-learning agents that detect, classify, and correct cell-level segmentation errors in an episodic setting that can treat mixed merge and split errors.
ocar.resolution: On CREMI tests, three variants beat Haehn-style sliding-window proofreading: mean CREMI score improved by 26.5% on set A, 54.6% on B, and 50.7% on C, with execution time down 95.7%, 94.7%, and 94.6% for Locator-Selector, Sliding-Static, and Sliding-Selector. The selector mainly improved correction quality; the locator mainly cut runtime.
ocar.future_work: They plan a continuous action space for small fragments and an extension from 2D-style patches to three dimensions.

summaries.beginner: Computers that outline cells in electron-microscope pictures still glue cells together or break them apart by mistake, and people usually fix that by hand. This paper trains a set of learning agents to find and repair those mistakes automatically.
summaries.intermediate: In 2021 work on arXiv (2106.05487), Nguyen, Jang, Tuan, and Jeong present RLCorrector, a hierarchy of reinforcement-learning agents for automatic EM proofreading. Compared with Haehn’s methods, CREMI scores improved 26.5%/54.6%/50.7% on sets A/B/C and runtimes fell about 95%. Visual cases show the locator spotting error patches and the selector choosing merge versus split agents.
summaries.advanced: Gains are versus a specific interactive baseline, not versus modern 3D agglomeration. Discrete actions struggle with small fragments; 3D is future work. The selected PDF is an arXiv preprint without journal pagination. Catalog method is electron microscopy at segmentation/proofreading/infrastructure stages.

plain_language_summary: Computers that outline cells in electron-microscope pictures still glue cells together or break them apart by mistake, and people usually fix that by hand. This paper trains a set of learning agents to find and repair those mistakes automatically.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroendocrine cells maintain homeostasis and stress responses, but the synaptic inputs that drive those outputs in the brain are less mapped than the hormones they release.
ocar.challenge: Without a complete wiring diagram onto endocrine projection neurons, combinatorial sensory control of peptide release remains schematic.
ocar.action: Hückesfeld, Schlegel, Miroschnikow, Schoofs, Zinke, Haubrich, Schneider-Mizell, Truman, Fetter, Cardona, and Pankratz use the TEM reconstruction of an entire Drosophila larval CNS to trace sensory and interneuron inputs onto neurosecretory cells that project to endocrine organs.
ocar.resolution: Network modeling predicted a previously undescribed carbon dioxide-responsive pathway onto a specific secretory set that includes corazonin (Crz) and diuretic hormone 44 (Dh44) cells. The architecture is combinatorial: sensory and interneuron paths converge onto distinct combinations of neuroendocrine outputs (ring-gland projection neurons).
ocar.future_work: The discussion highlights unique features such as eclosion-hormone neurons’ broad SEZ/VNC coupling, tied to cuticle shedding, as a target for further circuit work.

summaries.beginner: Hormone-releasing brain cells keep the body stable, but it is often unclear which sensory paths tell them when to fire. Using a complete larval fruit-fly wiring map, the authors trace those incoming paths and find a carbon-dioxide-related route onto particular peptide cells.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2021), Hückesfeld and colleagues reconstruct synaptic inputs onto Drosophila larval neurosecretory cells from the TEM whole-CNS connectome. They report a CO2-responsive network, predicted by modeling, that targets secretory cells including Crz and Dh44, and they describe combinatorial convergence of sensory and interneuron pathways onto distinct ring-gland projection neuron combinations.
summaries.advanced: “New” CO2 network is predicted by modeling then identified in the connectome; the selected extract does not quantify physiology. Catalog dimension is image-acquisition/TEM, but the contribution is circuit analysis of an existing larval TEM volume. Organism is larval fly, not adult.

plain_language_summary: Hormone-releasing brain cells keep the body stable, but it is often unclear which sensory paths tell them when to fire. Using a complete larval fruit-fly wiring map, the authors trace those incoming paths and find a carbon-dioxide-related route onto particular peptide cells.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM connectomes contain not only synapses but also cell morphologies and spatial distributions that are rarely explored interactively at whole-brain scale.
ocar.challenge: Terabyte ssEM volumes are hard to browse: 2D sections, 3D renderings, and segmentation tables usually live in separate tools, and filtering nuclei by shape or anatomy is cumbersome.
ocar.action: Choi, Hildebrand, Moon, Quan, Tuan, Ko, and Jeong introduce ZeVis, combining 2D cross-sections and 3D volumes of larval zebrafish ssEM with overlaid segmentations and a graph-based interface to subset objects by morphology or anatomical masks.
ocar.resolution: They apply ZeVis to a terabyte-scale whole larval zebrafish brain and analyze cell-nucleus distributions across anatomical regions.
ocar.future_work: They suggest interactive, ROI-limited segmentation inside the viewer, and restricting analyses to neurons, glia, or progenitors rather than all nuclei.

summaries.beginner: A whole baby-zebrafish brain imaged in electron microscopy is enormous and hard to look through. The authors built a viewing system that shows slices and 3D shapes together so scientists can count and compare cell nuclei in different brain regions.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Access (2021), Choi, Hildebrand, Moon, Quan, Tuan, Ko, and Jeong present ZeVis for a terabyte-scale larval zebrafish serial-section EM volume. The system links 2D and 3D views with segmentation overlays and graph-based filtering by morphological features or anatomical constraints, demonstrated on nucleus distributions. Background text notes typical ssEM resolution of 4–50 nm per voxel edge.
summaries.advanced: The 4–50 nm and 1 mm³/petabyte/100,000 cells/1 billion synapses figures are general ssEM scaling, not measurements of this zebrafish volume. Analyses use precomputed nucleus segmentations and region masks; generating those remains a workflow bottleneck they acknowledge. Catalog organism is zebrafish; method is serial-section EM.

plain_language_summary: A whole baby-zebrafish brain imaged in electron microscopy is enormous and hard to look through. The authors built a viewing system that shows slices and 3D shapes together so scientists can count and compare cell nuclei in different brain regions.

ocar.opportunity: Local circuits and the global connectome emerge from development, so explaining adult C. elegans wiring and behavior requires a developmental account of how cells acquire identities and synapses.
ocar.challenge: Preferential-attachment stories of complex networks do not obviously match biphasic growth of cell number across embryonic and postembryonic life, and the strategies by which neurons choose synaptic partners during larval synaptogenesis are underspecified.
ocar.action: Alicea synthesizes C. elegans developmental cell biology into “connectogenesis” and applies a first-mover Stackelberg competition model to larval chemical-synapse data, assigning heuristic pre/post strategies and comparing them with rich-club and NSY-5-related structure.
ocar.resolution: Potential pre- and postsynaptic roles yield distinct connection strategies argued to generalize to other small connectomes. Of 14 rich-club neurons, 10 prefer overlapping N–P coupling and XOR second-mover strategies; rich-club cells tend to be born between 290 and 350 minutes, so birth order alone does not explain their hub status.
ocar.future_work: Open questions include whether rich clubs arise from preferential attachment or from functional roles, and how to build biologically based models of developmental connectomics for systems such as Ciona.

summaries.beginner: The adult worm’s wiring diagram grows from a developing embryo, not all at once. This article argues that the order in which cells mature, and simple competitive rules for who synapses first, help explain that adult pattern.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience (2020; catalog journal field lists bioRxiv), Bradly Alicea presents an opinion-and-analysis synthesis of C. elegans connectogenesis. A first-mover Stackelberg model of larval synaptogenesis assigns strategies to potential pre- and postsynaptic partners. Ten of 14 adult rich-club neurons share N–P coupling and XOR second-mover strategies; those hubs are typically born at 290–350 min, so timing is not a simple preferential-attachment rule. Implications are drawn for simulation and other small connectomes.
summaries.advanced: This is explicitly framed as an opinion piece with a model demonstration, not new EM. Strategy labels (N–P, XOR, XNOR) are heuristic assignments. Catalog year/title match the Frontiers article; DOI is 10.3389/fncel.2020.524791. Dimension is neuroai/modeling on elegans.

plain_language_summary: The adult worm’s wiring diagram grows from a developing embryo, not all at once. This article argues that the order in which cells mature, and simple competitive rules for who synapses first, help explain that adult pattern.

ocar.opportunity: Graph analyses of nervous systems usually omit connection sign, yet excitatory/inhibitory balance is central to function, and C. elegans offers a directed chemical-synapse connectome plus neuron-resolved expression.
ocar.challenge: Whole-brain synaptic polarity is experimentally incomplete; neurotransmitter identity of the presynaptic cell is not enough because some receptors invert conventional excitation or inhibition.
ocar.action: Fenyves, Szilágyi, Vassy, Sőti, and Csermely predict ionotropic chemical-synapse signs from presynaptic transmitter and postsynaptic receptor expression for three major transmitter systems, releasing EleganSign (http://EleganSign.linkgroup.hu).
ocar.resolution: They cover more than two-thirds of 3,638 connections (20,589 synapses) among 302 neurons and obtain an excitatory:inhibitory ratio near 4:1 (about 20% negative edges), similar to several neural and social signed networks. Fourteen receptor genes encoding unconventional polarities are required for that ratio.
ocar.future_work: They note the method can incorporate spatial and temporal expression dynamics to study plasticity of E:I balance, and that the tool applies to any network with an expression atlas.

summaries.beginner: Whether a worm synapse turns the next cell on or off is often unknown. This paper guesses those plus and minus signs from which transmitters and receptors each cell makes, and finds about four excitatory connections for every inhibitory one.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS Computational Biology (2020), Fenyves and colleagues predict signs of the C. elegans ionotropic chemical connectome (3,638 connections, 20,589 synapses) from transmitter/receptor expression. Predictions cover more than two-thirds of those synapses and yield E:I close to 4:1 (20% negative edges). Unconventional receptors (inhibitory glutamate/acetylcholine or excitatory GABA) are essential to that balance. EleganSign is open source.
summaries.advanced: Predictions are expression-based, not electrophysiologically validated at whole-brain scale. Coverage is “more than two-thirds,” not all synapses; neuromodulatory and metabotropic routes are outside the ionotropic scope. Catalog journal field says bioRxiv; the PDF is the published PLOS article. Organism is elegans; stage is graph_analysis.

plain_language_summary: Whether a worm synapse turns the next cell on or off is often unknown. This paper guesses those plus and minus signs from which transmitters and receptors each cell makes, and finds about four excitatory connections for every inhibitory one.

ocar.opportunity: At about 150,000 neurons, the adult Drosophila CNS is near a complete cellular catalogue, but that catalogue is usable only if neurons are grouped into types of 1–1000 cells per hemisphere.
ocar.challenge: Type definitions must reconcile lineage, gene expression, morphology, connectivity, physiology, and behavior, and matching transcriptomic clusters to morphologies brain-wide remains unfinished.
ocar.action: Bates, Janssens, Jefferis, and Aerts review how anatomy and single-cell genomics are being combined to discover fly neuronal types at scale.
ocar.resolution: They argue that initial comparisons find morphological and transcriptomic types highly consistent, and that matched single-cell transcriptomes and morphologies can serve as a reference to integrate connectomics and to enable molecular-genetic access for functional prediction.
ocar.future_work: They identify brain-wide matching of the two modalities as the outstanding task.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly brains have about 150,000 cells, too many to think about one by one unless similar cells are grouped into types. This review explains how cell shape and gene activity are being used together to make those groups.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Bates, Janssens, Jefferis, and Aerts review neuronal cell-type discovery in Drosophila. They note types ranging from 1 to 1000 cells per hemisphere and that multiple co-varying properties—lineage, expression, morphology, connectivity, responses, and behavior—define type. Early morphology–transcriptome comparisons look consistent; matched atlases should help interpret connectomes and target genetic reagents.
summaries.advanced: Selected PDF text did not match this review (extract is a 2025 bioRxiv on a brain-and-cord connectome), so this annotation uses the catalog abstract only. The review is narrative, not a new atlas. “Highly consistent” is qualitative. Catalog tags fly cell-types and graph_analysis.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly brains have about 150,000 cells, too many to think about one by one unless similar cells are grouped into types. This review explains how cell shape and gene activity are being used together to make those groups.

ocar.opportunity: Circuit function depends on features spanning about 20 orders of magnitude of volume, from brain-wide projections to molecular synapses, and “neurocartography” aims to map those layers.
ocar.challenge: Full synaptic-scale mammalian brain reconstruction is argued to be decades away, so complementary light-microscopy strategies are needed to extract hodological principles at meso-, micro-, and nanoscales before a complete EM connectome exists.
ocar.action: Bloss and Hunt review array tomography and related light-microscopy methods for long-range and subcellular synaptic organization, and two-photon serial tomography of the whole mouse brain for potential connectivity of defined cell types, alongside CRACM and all-optical mapping.
ocar.resolution: They discuss mesoscale projectome topology (citing quantitative cortical analyses such as Oh et al., 2014), evidence for structured connectivity at cellular and dendritic scales, and how those maps should pose sharper questions for future EM connectomes.
ocar.future_work: They ask what existing neurocartographic results would let the field interrogate an EM connectome more incisively, including branch-level versus sub-branch synaptic clustering.

summaries.beginner: Mapping every mammal synapse will take a very long time, but other microscopes can already chart which cell types project where and where synapses sit on dendrites. This review surveys those complementary mapping methods.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2019), Bloss and Hunt review multiscale neurocartography of mammalian circuits. They contrast invertebrate EM connectomes with the infeasibility of a full synaptic-scale mammalian brain map for decades, then cover array tomography, two-photon serial tomography, mGRASP, and CRACM/all-optical approaches. Examples include hippocampal synaptic organization and mesoscale cortical projectomes used to infer circuit topologies.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not new primary mapping. CRACM cannot distinguish silent synapses from absent input. Catalog tags mouse, array tomography, two-photon, preparation and graph_analysis. “~20 orders of magnitude” is the authors’ span for relevant brain structure, not a measured dataset size.

plain_language_summary: Mapping every mammal synapse will take a very long time, but other microscopes can already chart which cell types project where and where synapses sit on dendrites. This review surveys those complementary mapping methods.

ocar.opportunity: EM, calcium imaging, and X-ray microtomography now produce gigabyte-to-petabyte structural datasets that could yield synapse-level connectomes and cell maps, but many labs cannot store or process data at that scale.
ocar.challenge: Existing machine-vision pipelines are often not portable, not scalable, poorly documented, or tied to one hardware stack, so results are hard to reproduce or extend across laboratories and modalities.
ocar.action: Johnson, Wilt, Rodriguez, Norman-Tenazas, Rivera, Drenkow, Kleissas, LaGrow, Cowley, Downs, Matelsky, Hughes, Reilly, Wester, Dyer, Kording, and Gray-Roncal introduce SABER: containerized open-source modules, Common Workflow Language, Apache Airflow (CONDUIT), block-merge execution, and bossDB storage, demonstrated on EM synapse-level connectomes and XRM cell distributions.
ocar.resolution: They argue the same standardized modules can be reused across neuroimaging experiments and even other domains. SABER is Apache-2.0 at github.com/aplbrain/saber; demonstration data live in bossDB.
ocar.future_work: They highlight remaining needs for archive-agnostic I/O as users share pipelines across storage formats, and for cloud (AWS Batch/Kubernetes) versus local execution choices.

summaries.beginner: Huge brain pictures are useless if only one lab’s custom computer setup can run the analysis. This paper describes a shared, containerized workflow system so different labs can process large electron-microscope and X-ray brain datasets in a repeatable way.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Johnson and colleagues present SABER, a reproducible framework connecting containerized tools, CWL workflow descriptions, Airflow execution, and volumetric storage (bossDB). Exemplars estimate synapse-level connectomes from EM and cell distributions from X-ray microtomography. They compare SABER with CWL-Airflow, Toil, Galaxy, and Air-tasks, emphasizing neuroimaging-specific block-merge and workflow optimization. Code is at github.com/aplbrain/saber under Apache 2.0.
summaries.advanced: This is a framework preprint, not a new biological connectome. No quantitative reconstruction accuracy for the EM/XRM exemplars appears in the selected text. Catalog tags infrastructure, graph_analysis, and electron microscopy; organism is unspecified.

plain_language_summary: Huge brain pictures are useless if only one lab’s custom computer setup can run the analysis. This paper describes a shared, containerized workflow system so different labs can process large electron-microscope and X-ray brain datasets in a repeatable way.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomics requires not only neuron shapes but also synapse locations and the direction of connectivity, for both vertebrate dyadic synapses and fly polyadic synapses.
ocar.challenge: Most detectors do not jointly find clefts and direction; methods that do have typically been shown on only one synapse class, not both.
ocar.action: Parag, Berger, Kamentsky, Staffler, Wei, Helmstaedter, Lichtman, and Pfister predict signed voxel proximity with a 3D U-Net to propose candidates, then prune with a second 3D CNN, without hand-crafted features, and release EMSynConn.
ocar.resolution: They report better synapse detection than prior methods on rodent cortex versus SynEM and, as HCBS on CREMI TEM volumes (4×4×40 nm), a CREMI score of 0.449 (223.000 FP, 286.667 FN), second overall (0.002 behind first) and ahead of both IAL variants.
ocar.future_work: They suggest extending the pruner to a three-class excitatory/inhibitory distinction.

summaries.beginner: To turn an electron-microscope volume into a wiring diagram, a computer must find each contact and which cell is sending versus receiving. This paper trains two networks to mark those contacts in both mouse and fruit-fly tissue.
summaries.intermediate: In ECCV Workshops (2018; arXiv 1807.02739), Parag and colleagues detect synapse location and direction for dyadic and polyadic contacts via signed-proximity U-Net candidates plus CNN pruning. On mouse cortex they visually and quantitatively outperform SynEM (which they note used ground-truth segmentation for partners, whereas they used automatic segmentation). On CREMI, HCBS scored 0.449 versus IAL 0.461/0.464. Code: github.com/paragt/EMSynConn.
summaries.advanced: CREMI ranking is as of that submission (Tr66 80K); cleft pixel error is not their reported metric. Partner scoring used automatic segmentation on fly data. Catalog organism is fly and method includes U-Net/EM, though rodent experiments are equally central. Advanced three-class sign prediction is proposed, not demonstrated.

plain_language_summary: To turn an electron-microscope volume into a wiring diagram, a computer must find each contact and which cell is sending versus receiving. This paper trains two networks to mark those contacts in both mouse and fruit-fly tissue.

ocar.opportunity: In mammalian cortex, an estimated 70–90% of synapses in a local volume come from distant axons, so dense EM reconstructions need a way to color those long-range inputs.
ocar.challenge: EM itself has almost no color channels, and chemical conversion or fiducial marks are cumbersome for many fluorescently labeled projection classes.
ocar.action: Drawitsch, Karimi, Boergens, and Helmstaedter introduce FluoEM: correlate LM and EM, reconstruct axons, and match unique 3D trajectories computationally, virtually painting EM axons with fluorescence identities, demonstrated on long-distance input to mouse cortical layer 1 using SBEM.
ocar.resolution: They find axonal trajectories in dense cortical neuropil become unique by about 40–50 μm of EM extent (uniqueness length below 40 μm at the 90th percentile across several layers), without artificial fiducials or label conversion. The geometry-based match is in principle compatible with FIB-SEM and ATUM-SEM as well as SBEM.
ocar.future_work: Practical limits include how many fluorescence channels can be imaged before tissue damage (they mention hours of continuous LM) and longer uniqueness lengths in highly anisotropic bundles such as white matter.

summaries.beginner: Most of the wires entering a small piece of mouse cortex come from far away, but electron-microscope pictures are black-and-white. This method matches glowing axons from a light microscope to the same axons in the electron-microscope volume by the unique paths they take.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2018), Drawitsch, Karimi, Boergens, and Helmstaedter present FluoEM for virtual multicolor labeling of axons in dense mouse cortical EM. Matching relies on trajectory uniqueness over about 40–50 μm (90th percentile uniqueness length <40 μm in several cortical layers). They demonstrate identification of long-range input into layer 1 and argue the approach extends to FIB-SEM and ATUM-SEM. Distal synapses are cited as 70–90% of local cortical synapses (Stepanyants et al., 2009).
summaries.advanced: Uniqueness length is empirical for the cortical layers they measured, not a universal constant; white-matter-like anisotropy is expected to worsen it. Channel count is limited by LM-induced damage. Catalog organism is mouse; method is electron microscopy. This is a tools-and-resources paper, not a full long-range connectome.

plain_language_summary: Most of the wires entering a small piece of mouse cortex come from far away, but electron-microscope pictures are black-and-white. This method matches glowing axons from a light microscope to the same axons in the electron-microscope volume by the unique paths they take.

ocar.opportunity: Neuron segmentation from 3D EM is the accuracy and throughput bottleneck between imaging and a connectome, and a single method that works on both isotropic block-face and anisotropic serial-section data would scale further.
ocar.challenge: Affinity prediction must be topologically correct; the original MALIS structured loss was computationally heavy (quadratic) and could inject spurious early-training gradients, while agglomeration on weak affinities needed elaborate heuristics.
ocar.action: Funke, Tschopp, Grisaitis, Sheridan, Singh, Saalfeld, and Turaga train a 3D U-Net to predict voxel affinities with an extended MALIS loss (quasi-linear gradient, two-pass to avoid early spurious terms), then apply learning-free percentile agglomeration.
ocar.resolution: On three datasets (CREMI, FIB, SegEM) they report relative improvements of 27%, 15%, and 250% over previous results. Simple agglomeration beats more involved methods used on worse affinities. Runtime scales linearly at about 2.6 seconds per megavoxel.
ocar.future_work: They argue one 3D strategy can serve both nearly isotropic block-face and anisotropic serial-section EM at very large volumes.

summaries.beginner: Computers must trace every neuron through a 3D electron-microscope stack without breaking or gluing cells. This paper trains a network to judge which tiny voxels belong together, then groups them, and reports large accuracy gains on three test sets.
summaries.intermediate: In 2017 arXiv work (later TPAMI-style presentation in the extract), Funke and colleagues combine 3D U-Net affinities with structured MALIS loss and percentile agglomeration. A quasi-linear, two-pass gradient replaces quadratic MALIS. They report 27%, 15%, and 250% relative improvements on CREMI, FIB, and SegEM, linear scaling, and ~2.6 s/megavoxel, claiming the method fits both block-face and serial-section EM.
summaries.advanced: Relative improvements are dataset-specific; 250% especially should not be generalized. Catalog title is the original arXiv wording; the PDF uses a later title. Organism is unspecified. Agglomeration success is predicated on the improved affinities. UUID in the catalog is the work_id, not a DOI.

plain_language_summary: Computers must trace every neuron through a 3D electron-microscope stack without breaking or gluing cells. This paper trains a network to judge which tiny voxels belong together, then groups them, and reports large accuracy gains on three test sets.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics must span nanometers to long-range axons, but serial-section EM volumes are typically only hundreds of cubic microns, leaving cell identity and processes that leave the volume unknown.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy can follow genetically labeled arbors over millimeters but not synaptic partners; most CLEM methods still struggle to mark a single in vivo neuron’s membrane for targeted ATUM-SEM without ruining ultrastructure.
ocar.action: Hirabayashi, Tapia, and Polleux fuse APEX2 to membrane-targeted Venus (Apex2-Venus-CAAX), introduce it sparsely into pyramidal neurons by in utero cortical electroporation, map arbors with confocal microscopy, then target ATUM-SEM (CoLSSEM).
ocar.resolution: Short 5–10 minute H2O2/DAB development preserves membranes better than ~1.5 h HRP incubations. They reconstruct a labeled apical dendrite (256 sections at 30 nm/px to find the ROI, then 103 sections at 3 nm/px) including mitochondria. Dual LM-EM labeling from one protein aids correlation.
ocar.future_work: Limitations they flag: DAB precipitate can diffuse and obscure cytoplasm, especially in spines and fine axons. They present CoLSSEM as improving feasibility of targeted large-scale reconstructions of identified neurons.

summaries.beginner: A light microscope can follow one glowing neuron a long way, but only an electron microscope can see its synapses, and the two pictures are hard to match. The authors genetically stain a single mouse neuron so it is visible in both, then zoom the electron microscope onto that cell.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2018; catalog year 2017), Hirabayashi, Tapia, and Polleux introduce CoLSSEM: sparse in utero electroporation of membrane-targeted APEX2-Venus, confocal reconstruction, and targeted ATUM-SEM. DAB development is 5–10 minutes. Example imaging used 256 serial sections at 30 nm/px then 103 sections at 3 nm/px to reconstruct a labeled apical dendrite and mitochondria.
summaries.advanced: The method is demonstrated on sparsely labeled pyramidal neurons, not a dense circuit. DAB can obscure spine and fine-axon cytoplasm. Catalog year is 2017 (received 19 October 2017) while the article is Scientific Reports 8:14491 (2018). Organism is unspecified in the catalog; the preparation is mammalian cortex. Method tags include ATUM, serial-section EM, CLEM, and confocal.

plain_language_summary: A light microscope can follow one glowing neuron a long way, but only an electron microscope can see its synapses, and the two pictures are hard to match. The authors genetically stain a single mouse neuron so it is visible in both, then zoom the electron microscope onto that cell.

ocar.opportunity: Fly-scale EM volumes are terabytes; reconstructing neurons that may cross thousands of planes is years of manual work unless segmentation is distributed beyond a single machine.
ocar.challenge: Blockwise segmentation can be ruined by a single false merge, by classifiers that fail to generalize, or by image anomalies, and naive stitching plus disk I/O does not scale.
ocar.action: Plaza and Berg implement large-scale EM segmentation in Spark with a plugin architecture, in-memory segmentation representation, and robustness measures against merge/split disasters, reading and writing via DVID, applied to large FlyEM volumes.
ocar.resolution: They report that the design minimizes disk I/O, deploys on different clusters, and is robust to local segmentation failures that would otherwise compromise the global result. Algorithms are biased toward false splits, which are easier to proofread than false merges.
ocar.future_work: Future work includes using global in-memory context for new stitching algorithms and distributed DVID backends to remove remaining read/write bottlenecks.

summaries.beginner: A fruit-fly brain imaged at synapse resolution is too big for one computer to color in every neuron. This paper describes a cluster computing system that splits the work across many machines without one local mistake wrecking the whole map.
summaries.intermediate: In 2016 arXiv work, Plaza and Berg present Spark-based segmentation for terabyte EM volumes, motivated by fly data in which a 50-micron neuron may intersect thousands of planes. The system uses a plugin architecture, in-memory objects, and DVID, aiming to contain classifier or image-anomaly errors. They emphasize false-split bias because merges are harder to proofread. Acknowledgements credit Janelia FlyEM imaging and proofreading.
summaries.advanced: The extract does not report numeric VI/Rand scores or wall-clock scaling curves. “A few large EM datasets” are unnamed in the selected text. Catalog organism is fly; stages are segmentation and proofreading. UUID is the work_id.

plain_language_summary: A fruit-fly brain imaged at synapse resolution is too big for one computer to color in every neuron. This paper describes a cluster computing system that splits the work across many machines without one local mistake wrecking the whole map.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM can resolve all synapses, but saturated reconstruction of every process is often slower than needed for comparing identified cell types across animals.
ocar.challenge: Unlabeled neuropil forces uniform high-resolution imaging and heavy segmentation; genetically marked neurons are hard to make electron-dense enough for fast targeting without wrecking ultrastructure.
ocar.action: Joesch, Mankus, Yamagata, Shahbazi, Schalek, Suissa-Peleg, Meister, Lichtman, Scheirer, and Sanes deliver viral peroxidase tracers, a contrast-enhancing protocol that keeps ultrastructure, low-then-high resolution reimaging of labeled regions, and an unsupervised segmentation algorithm that exploits the extra contrast.
ocar.resolution: High contrast of marked cells enables targeted high-resolution reimaging and unsupervised segmentation, reducing imaging and reconstruction times by two orders of magnitude and supporting directed queries of circuit motifs. Data are deposited at Dryad.
ocar.future_work: The pipeline is offered for directed circuit-motif studies rather than as a replacement for fully saturated connectomes.

summaries.beginner: Reconstructing every wire in an electron-microscope stack is extremely slow. The authors genetically darken chosen neurons so the microscope can zoom only on those cells and a computer can trace them much faster.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2016), Joesch and colleagues reconstruct genetically identified neurons from serial-section EM using viral peroxidase derivatives and a staining protocol that boosts electron density while preserving ultrastructure. Targeted high-resolution reimaging of regions chosen from a fast low-resolution pass, plus unsupervised segmentation of the high-contrast cells, is reported to cut imaging and reconstruction time by two orders of magnitude.
summaries.advanced: “Two orders of magnitude” is a pipeline-level claim without a full timing table in the selected extract. Unsupervised segmentation relies on the enhanced contrast of labeled cells, not unlabeled neuropil. Catalog organism is unspecified; method is serial-section EM across sectioning, acquisition, segmentation, and graph_analysis. AAV constructs are listed in supplements.

plain_language_summary: Reconstructing every wire in an electron-microscope stack is extremely slow. The authors genetically darken chosen neurons so the microscope can zoom only on those cells and a computer can trace them much faster.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans connectome is a unique whole-animal graph in which one can ask which neurons and synapses are architecturally critical for information processing.
ocar.challenge: It remains unclear how efficiently shared pathways still support distinct behaviors, and which cells are control points versus merely high-degree nodes.
ocar.action: Kim, Kim, Kralik, and Jeong computationally “attack” 279 neurons and 2,990 weighted connections (6,393 chemical synapses and 890 electrical junctions), scoring effects on global clustering, efficiency, and betweenness.
ocar.resolution: They identify 12 critical neurons and 29 critical synapses that behave as control elements influencing many pathways. Critical synapses assemble into circuits related to backward locomotion (AVA-based), avoidance, and social feeding, supporting a mixed parallel-and-serial architecture.
ocar.future_work: From an evo-devo view they suggest new clustering, efficiency, and betweenness would be most affected by adding paired neighbor synapses, central shortcuts, and chains of control units, respectively.

summaries.beginner: If you knock out one worm neuron or synapse in a computer model, some removals barely matter and a few scramble the whole network. This study finds a small set of those high-impact cells and links, including ones used for backing up.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS Computational Biology (2016), Kim, Kim, Kralik, and Jeong attack the C. elegans connectome node-by-node and edge-by-edge (279 neurons; 2,990 weighted connections from 6,393 chemical synapses and 890 gap junctions). Twelve neurons and 29 synapses are critical for clustering, integration, and propagation; they interpret these as control elements. Emergent pathways implicate backward locomotion, avoidance, and social feeding, and a mixed parallel/serial design.
summaries.advanced: Criticality is with respect to chosen graph metrics after single removals, not behavioral knockout phenocopy. Weighted connections (2,990) compress multiple synapses. Catalog stage is graph_analysis on elegans. Claims about biological importance of backward locomotion are inferences from network influence, not new experiments.

plain_language_summary: If you knock out one worm neuron or synapse in a computer model, some removals barely matter and a few scramble the whole network. This study finds a small set of those high-impact cells and links, including ones used for backing up.

ocar.opportunity: Light and electron microscopes can produce terascale 3D images in hours, so segmentation algorithms need near-linear runtime and a way to tame watershed oversegmentation.
ocar.challenge: Classic watershed is linear but badly oversegments; agglomeration must use prior knowledge of object sizes without introducing mergers.
ocar.action: Zlateski and Seung define a disaffinity graph, compute a linear-time watershed on edge-weighted graphs with even plateau splits, build a basin graph, and merge with size-dependent single-linkage clustering, optionally thresholding edges before watershed.
ocar.resolution: On 3D EM brain images with convolutional-net disaffinities, size-dependent linkage reduced oversegmentation versus Felzenszwalb-style clustering on either the voxel graph or the basin graph, with “virtually no mergers” in their conclusion. Example threshold ω(w)=3000(1−w). Rand split/merge scores are shown against human ground truth.
ocar.future_work: They present the quasilinear method as suitable for very large images.

summaries.beginner: A common computer method floods an image like a landscape and cuts it into too many tiny pieces. This paper merges those pieces using rules about how big real objects should be, so brain scans can be segmented quickly without wrongly gluing neurons together.
summaries.intermediate: In 2015 arXiv work, Zlateski and Seung segment images via watershed basins on a disaffinity graph followed by size-dependent single-linkage clustering of the basin graph. Runtime is quasilinear. Illustrated on 3D EM with conv-net affinities, their size functions outperform Felzenszwalb clustering at comparable merge rates, reducing splits. They conclude oversegmentation can be cut while introducing virtually no mergers.
summaries.advanced: “Virtually no mergers” is the authors’ summary of their parameter setting, not a zero-error guarantee on held-out connectomes. Scores are on one illustrated EM volume with human ground truth restricted to foreground voxels. Catalog methods include structured-loss affinity segmentation and volume EM; organism is unspecified. UUID is the work_id.

plain_language_summary: A common computer method floods an image like a landscape and cuts it into too many tiny pieces. This paper merges those pieces using rules about how big real objects should be, so brain scans can be segmented quickly without wrongly gluing neurons together.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic efficacy correlates strongly with anatomy, so the precision of spine geometry can bound how much information a synapse can store through plasticity.
ocar.challenge: Many noise sources affect synapses; without pairs that share pre- and postsynaptic history, one cannot separate plasticity precision from independent variation.
ocar.action: Bartol, Bromer, Kinney, Chirillo, Bourne, Harris, and Sejnowski reconstruct hippocampal neuropil and analyze axon-coupled spine pairs (same axon, same dendrite) as shared-history controls.
ocar.resolution: Spine head volumes and neck diameters, but not neck lengths, of those pairs were nearly identical. They infer a minimum of 26 distinguishable synaptic strengths, or 4.7 bits per synapse. That precision would require averaging stochastic activity over several minutes. Among 287 synapses, 17 axon-coupled pairs were as closely matched as a 1-in-5000 chance for random pairs (KS p=0.0002); neck-diameter r²=0.70.
ocar.future_work: They note that more samples would confirm and extend the bound, and they contrast their anatomical variability estimate as an order of magnitude lower than some neocortical physiological reports.

summaries.beginner: Some synapses on a neuron are big and some are small, which may be how memories are stored. By finding pairs of contacts that have always been used together, the authors show those pairs are almost the same size, meaning the brain can set synapse strength very precisely.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2015), Bartol, Bromer, Kinney, Chirillo, Bourne, Harris, and Sejnowski use EM of hippocampal neuropil to compare axon-coupled spine pairs. Heads and neck diameters match closely; neck lengths do not. They estimate at least 26 distinguishable strengths (4.7 bits) per synapse, requiring minutes of averaging given stochastic release. Seventeen such pairs among 287 synapses yield KS p=0.0002 versus random pairing.
summaries.advanced: Bits and distinguishable-strength counts are model-based lower bounds from anatomical variance, not measured information throughput. n=17 pairs is small despite a strong p-value. Correlation of PSD area and docked vesicles with head size is expected from prior literature. Catalog organism is unspecified; method is electron microscopy. Hippocampal CA1-type neuropil should not be assumed cortex-wide.

plain_language_summary: Some synapses on a neuron are big and some are small, which may be how memories are stored. By finding pairs of contacts that have always been used together, the authors show those pairs are almost the same size, meaning the brain can set synapse strength very precisely.

ocar.opportunity: Molecularly defined cell types are the nodes of many modern circuit maps, but serial-section EM still struggles to tag synapses of a chosen genotype while keeping ultrastructure.
ocar.challenge: Long-range axons of genetically specified hypothalamic neurons (AGRP and POMC feeding circuits) cannot be followed into dense neuropil by light microscopy alone, and conventional EM labels often damage tissue or lack genetic control in mouse and fly.
ocar.action: Atasoy, Betley, Li, Su, Sertel, Scheffer, Simpson, Fetter, and Sternson introduce GESEM: intra-vesicular HRP fused to VAMP2/nSyb generates electron-dense bouton labeling in Cre- or GAL4-dependent neurons, then combine selective EM reconstruction with functional and viral mapping.
ocar.resolution: The label identified synapses from molecularly defined neurons in mouse and fly with preserved ultrastructure. Applied to AGRP and POMC projections, it revealed basic organizational features of those long-range feeding circuits.
ocar.future_work: They suggest pairing GESEM with dual pre/post labels and functional mapping to build cell-type-specific connectomes.

summaries.beginner: Scientists can genetically mark hunger-related brain cells, but seeing their tiny synapses in an electron microscope usually destroys the tissue or loses the genetic label. This paper puts an enzyme inside the cells’ release packets so those synapses show up as dark spots without ruining the structure.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2014), Atasoy, Betley, Li, Su, Sertel, Scheffer, Simpson, Fetter, and Sternson present GESEM (VAMP2:HRP / nSyb:HRP) for Cre- or GAL4-dependent electron-dense labeling of boutons in mouse and Drosophila. They apply it to long-range AGRP and POMC hypothalamic projections, combining selective neuropil reconstruction with ChR2 and viral circuit mapping to describe projection organization. The Cre-dependent AAV construct was deposited at Addgene.
summaries.advanced: This is a targeted, not saturated, reconstruction of labeled boutons. “Some basic features” of AGRP/POMC organization are not quantified in the selected extract. Catalog stages list sectioning on mouse with serial-section EM; fly GAL4 labeling is also demonstrated. Methods detail ARC injection coordinates and housing, not synapse counts.

plain_language_summary: Scientists can genetically mark hunger-related brain cells, but seeing their tiny synapses in an electron microscope usually destroys the tissue or loses the genetic label. This paper puts an enzyme inside the cells’ release packets so those synapses show up as dark spots without ruining the structure.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics had been applied to few species; pycnogonids (sea spiders) occupy a key place in arthropod phylogeny, so their visual neuropils can test whether median-eye and lateral-eye circuit motifs generalize.
ocar.challenge: Serial TEM of entire neurons needs hundreds of lossless sections, elastic alignment, and still has ~70 nm z sampling; volumes of thousands of cubic micrometers at few-nanometer voxels are demanding.
ocar.action: Lehmann, Heß, Wanner, and Melzer use FIB-SEM (z resolution down to 5 nm, aligned stacks without section loss) to reconstruct the visual connectome of Achelia langi, complemented by Golgi impregnations.
ocar.resolution: Each eye-tubercle hemisphere’s two eyes map to first and second visual neuropils; the first is two hemineuropils with three layers. Six postsynaptic neuron types are described (five descending unipolar, one ascending). Chemical-synapse mapping indicates descending cells are second-order to retinula axons; ascending cells are mostly presynaptic onto R-cells and may provide feedback. They conclude the system mixes chelicerate median-eye and mandibulate lateral-eye features.
ocar.future_work: The study is positioned as expanding connectomics beyond classic models rather than as a whole-animal connectome.

summaries.beginner: Sea spiders have simple eyes whose inner wiring had not been mapped at synapse scale. Using a focused-ion-beam electron microscope, the authors reconstruct those visual centers and find circuit parts that look like both spider-style and insect-style eyes.
summaries.intermediate: In BMC Biology (2014), Lehmann, Heß, Wanner, and Melzer reconstruct Achelia langi visual neuropils with FIB-SEM. Two eyes per hemisphere innervate layered first and second neuropils. Six morphological neuron types postsynaptic to R-cells are matched to Golgi material; synapse mapping assigns descending unipolar neurons as second-order and ascending neurons as largely feedback. They compare this organization with crustacean and insect compound-eye circuits.
summaries.advanced: This is a regional visual connectome, not a whole-CNS map. Catalog organism is tagged elegans, which does not match the sea spider subject; method is FIB-SEM. “All identifiable chemical synapses” is limited to the reconstructed visual neuropil. Phylogenetic interpretation (median vs lateral eye features) is comparative morphology, not a molecular phylogeny in this paper.

plain_language_summary: Sea spiders have simple eyes whose inner wiring had not been mapped at synapse scale. Using a focused-ion-beam electron microscope, the authors reconstruct those visual centers and find circuit parts that look like both spider-style and insect-style eyes.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation (here, the Rhoana pipeline) still errs, so dense connectomes on terabyte serial-section volumes need interactive correction that stays usable at that scale.
ocar.challenge: Existing reconstruction tools were not all designed for dense proofreading of automatic labels on TB data; interaction cost dominates 3D reconstruction time.
ocar.action: Knowles-Barley, Roberts, Kasthuri, Lee, Pfister, and Lichtman present Mojo 2.0, an open-source desktop annotator in which sparse scribbles merge split objects or watershed-split merged objects in 2D or 3D, with predicted splits propagated across adjacent sections.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate the tool on mouse cortical SSEM labeled by Rhoana and compare the workflow with manual tracing. An adjust mode covers mixed split-and-merge fixes. The application lists segments by size and scales toward TB volumes. Software was offered at rhoana.org.
ocar.future_work: The conference abstract frames Mojo 2.0 as a demonstration of interaction modes rather than a completed whole-cortex connectome.

summaries.beginner: Computers that color neurons in electron-microscope pictures still make mistakes, and fixing a trillion-pixel stack by painting every pixel is hopeless. This tool lets a person scribble a few strokes to join or split those computer labels.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2013 Frontiers Neuroinformatics conference abstract, Knowles-Barley, Roberts, Kasthuri, Lee, Pfister, and Lichtman describe Mojo 2.0 for correcting automatic EM segmentations. Sparse scribbles merge objects or split them along membranes via watershed; splits can propagate in 3D while preserving connectivity. They demo mouse cortex SSEM from the Rhoana pipeline versus manual tracing. The tool is open source and aimed at TB-scale volumes.
summaries.advanced: This is a short conference demonstration, not a methods journal article with benchmark tables. No numeric proofreading-speedup appears in the extract. Catalog journal is empty; DOI is 10.3389/conf.fninf.2013.09.00060. Stages span segmentation, proofreading, infrastructure, and graph_analysis; organism is unspecified though the demo is mouse cortex.

plain_language_summary: Computers that color neurons in electron-microscope pictures still make mistakes, and fixing a trillion-pixel stack by painting every pixel is hopeless. This tool lets a person scribble a few strokes to join or split those computer labels.

ocar.opportunity: Fly and vertebrate brains share layers, columns, glomeruli, and many synaptic molecules, so Drosophila is a place to read out synaptic circuits cell by cell and then add function with genetics.
ocar.challenge: Structural connectomes, molecular parts lists, and physiology still sit in separate literatures; recording alone shows correlates of behavior rather than causal necessity of identified neurons.
ocar.action: Meinertzhagen and Lee review serial-section EM and related imaging for the fly connectome, plus genetic reagents that identify transmitters, receptors, and transporters and that record or manipulate activity.
ocar.resolution: They argue that combining anatomical networks with genetic disruption—blocking or rescuing identified neurons—can establish causal bases of behavior in ways correlative electro- or optophysiology cannot, and they survey the reagent landscape needed as connectomic data grow.
ocar.future_work: They predict a union of network anatomy and genetic perturbation as the core of functional connectomics, while noting space limits prevented citing many relevant studies.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies now have increasingly complete wiring maps, and genetic tricks can turn identified cells off or on. This review explains how combining those maps with those tricks can show which cells actually cause a behavior, not merely which cells are active when it happens.
summaries.intermediate: In Advances in Genetics (2012), Meinertzhagen and Lee review functional connectomics in Drosophila. They emphasize shared organizational motifs with vertebrates, the emerging ability of EM to yield cell-by-cell pathways, and genetic tools for synaptic components and activity. The concluding argument is causal: only neuron-specific block or rescue, not recording alone, probes a neuron’s role in behavior.
summaries.advanced: This is a wide-ranging review, not a new connectome. Causal-versus-correlative rhetoric is a stance, not a methods comparison with quantified false-causal rates. Catalog method is electron microscopy on fly; no pipeline stage is tagged. The NIH-PA manuscript extract is the author manuscript of the 2012 chapter (80:99–151).

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies now have increasingly complete wiring maps, and genetic tricks can turn identified cells off or on. This review explains how combining those maps with those tricks can show which cells actually cause a behavior, not merely which cells are active when it happens.
